# The Five Faculties

*SN 48.10, the Dutiyavibhaṅga Sutta — set 5, Advanced and Reference Texts*

<p class="reading-meta"><strong>Reading time:</strong> about 4 min · 643 words</p>

[Skip to the translation](#translation){ .reader-skip-link }

## Before you read

Five words that sound like personality traits — confidence, energy,
remembering, composure, discernment — and not one of them is defined here as a
trait. Every answer starts the same way, with a person, and then describes
something being done. Confidence is placed somewhere specific, for reasons the
text spells out. Energy is four efforts, named one at a time. Remembering is
recalling what was said long ago, and also watching four things as they happen.

The definitions get longer as the list goes on, and the last one turns out to
be the four noble truths — which puts the whole list inside the path rather
than somewhere before it.

This is a reference text. Read it straight through once to see the shape, then
come back to whichever of the five you were least sure about.

## Translation

### The Five Faculties

"Bhikkhus, there are these five faculties.

What five? The faculty of confidence ... the faculty of discernment.

### The Faculty of Confidence

And what, bhikkhus, is the faculty of confidence?

Here a noble disciple has confidence. They place confidence in the awakening
of the Tathāgata: 'So indeed is the Buddha — an arahant, perfectly and fully
awakened, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, well-departed, knower of the
world, unsurpassed guide for those to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans,
awakened, blessed.'

This, bhikkhus, is called the faculty of confidence.

### The Faculty of Energy

And what, bhikkhus, is the faculty of energy?

Here a noble disciple lives with aroused energy for the abandoning of
unwholesome qualities and the taking up of wholesome qualities — steadfast,
firm in exertion, not putting down the burden with respect to wholesome
qualities.

They generate desire for the non-arising of unarisen harmful, unwholesome
qualities; they make an effort, arouse energy, take hold of the heart,
and exert themselves.

They generate desire for the abandoning of arisen harmful, unwholesome
qualities; they make an effort, arouse energy, take hold of the heart,
and exert themselves.

They generate desire for the arising of unarisen wholesome qualities; they
make an effort, arouse energy, take hold of the heart, and exert
themselves.

They generate desire for the continuation, non-confusion, increase,
abundance, development, and fulfilment of arisen wholesome qualities; they
make an effort, arouse energy, take hold of the heart, and exert
themselves.

This, bhikkhus, is called the faculty of energy.

### The Faculty of Remembering

And what, bhikkhus, is the faculty of remembering?

Here a noble disciple remembers. They possess the highest carefulness in
remembering, and they recall and call to mind what was done and said long ago.

They remain observing the body in relation to the body, ardent, with clear
knowing, with remembering, having removed coveting and distress regarding the
world.

They remain observing felt experience ...

They remain observing the heart ...

They remain observing dhammas among dhammas, ardent, with clear knowing, with
remembering, having removed coveting and distress regarding the world.

This, bhikkhus, is called the faculty of remembering.

### The Faculty of Composure

And what, bhikkhus, is the faculty of composure?

Here a noble disciple, having made relinquishment the object, gains composure,
gains directness of heart.

Quite secluded from sensuality, secluded from unwholesome dhammas, they enter
and remain in the first mental theme, which has thinking and pondering, and
the rejoicing and satisfaction born of seclusion.

With the subsiding of thinking and pondering, with inner clarity and
unification of the heart, they enter and remain in the second mental
theme, without thinking and pondering, with the rejoicing and satisfaction
born of composure.

With the fading of rejoicing, they remain in dynamic balance, remembering and
clearly knowing, and experience satisfaction in the body. They enter and
remain in the third mental theme, of which the noble ones say: 'One of dynamic
balance and remembering stays satisfied.'

With the abandoning of satisfaction and discomfort, and with the earlier
ending of gladness and sadness, they enter and remain in the fourth mental
theme, without discomfort and without satisfaction, purified by dynamic
balance and remembering.

This, bhikkhus, is called the faculty of composure.

### The Faculty of Discernment

And what, bhikkhus, is the faculty of discernment?

Here a noble disciple discerns. They possess the discernment that leads to
arising and passing away — noble, penetrating, rightly leading to the wearing
away of dissatisfaction.

They discern it as it has come to be: 'This is dissatisfaction.' They discern
it as it has come to be: 'This is the origin of dissatisfaction.' They discern
it as it has come to be: 'This is the quenching of dissatisfaction.' They
discern it as it has come to be: 'This is the way of practice leading to the
quenching of dissatisfaction.'

This, bhikkhus, is called the faculty of discernment.

These, bhikkhus, are the five faculties."

<dd>This translation&#x27;s rendering of &quot;dukkha,&quot; the Buddhist term for the unsatisfying, unstable quality of ordinary experience. Often translated &quot;suffering,&quot; but that can sound more dramatic than the everyday sense of things not quite being right.</dd>
<dt><dfn>dynamic balance</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;upekkhā&quot; (often translated &quot;equanimity&quot;) -- a steadiness that stays engaged rather than checking out, distinct from indifference.</dd>

<dd>The fading away of attraction and investment in experience, as passion cools.</dd>

<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;vedanā&quot; (often translated &quot;feeling&quot;) -- the immediate pleasant, unpleasant, or neutral tone of an experience, prior to any story built on top of it.</dd>

<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;muditā&quot; (often translated &quot;sympathetic joy&quot;) -- being genuinely glad at someone else&#x27;s good fortune, cultivated as a practice rather than assumed to come naturally.</dd>

<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;citta&quot; -- the affective or feeling side of mind: the part that takes on a mood, wants, leans, reacts, and can be gladdened, steadied, trained, and released. <dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;jhāna&quot; -- a single theme the mind rests on and holds steadily. Described in a sequence of four, each calmer than the last. Most translations leave the word in Pāli.</dd>

*[arahant]: Someone who has completed the path and has nothing further to do. Left untranslated; "saint" and "perfected one" both mislead.
*[awakening]: Coming fully awake to how things are. Sometimes translated "enlightenment," a word this project avoids as needlessly mystical.
*[bhikkhus]: Buddhist monks -- those who have left household life to practise full time. The Buddha's usual way of addressing the assembly, roughly "friends" in force.
*[body]: The physical body. In MN 63 specifically, paired with "soul" in one of the undeclared questions.
*[born of seclusion]: Coming from having stepped away from busyness and distraction, rather than from anything acquired.
*[clear knowing]: Knowing plainly what you are doing while you are doing it.
*[clearly knowing]: Acting while plainly aware of what you are doing.
*[composure]: This project's rendering of "samādhi" -- the thinking mind and heart collected together and working in accord rather than pulling against each other. It is a settled, coherent, workable condition fit for practice. Usually translated "concentration," which this project avoids because it suggests forcing and strain.
*[dissatisfaction]: This translation's rendering of "dukkha," the Buddhist term for the unsatisfying, unstable quality of ordinary experience. Often translated "suffering," but that can sound more dramatic than the everyday sense of things not quite being right.
*[dynamic balance]: This project's rendering of "upekkhā" (often translated "equanimity") -- a steadiness that stays engaged rather than checking out, distinct from indifference.
*[fading]: The fading away of attraction and investment in experience, as passion cools.
*[felt experience]: This project's rendering of "vedanā" (often translated "feeling") -- the immediate pleasant, unpleasant, or neutral tone of an experience, prior to any story built on top of it.
*[gladness]: This project's rendering of "muditā" (often translated "sympathetic joy") -- being genuinely glad at someone else's good fortune, cultivated as a practice rather than assumed to come naturally.
*[heart]: This project's rendering of "citta" -- the affective or feeling side of mind: the part that takes on a mood, wants, leans, reacts, and can be gladdened, steadied, trained, and released. It is sometimes called the "heart-mind" or "feeling mind"; here "heart" does not mean merely emotion or the physical organ.
*[knowing]: This project's rendering of "viññāṇa" (often translated "consciousness") -- bare awareness of an object through one of the senses or the mind.
*[mental theme]: This project's rendering of "jhāna" -- a single theme the mind rests on and holds steadily. Described in a sequence of four, each calmer than the last. Most translations leave the word in Pāli.
*[noble disciple]: Someone who has had the breakthrough into the path and so is no longer merely an ordinary person. It does not mean noble by birth, and does not require being a monastic.
*[quenching]: The ending of dissatisfaction and its causes, and its underlying causes going out like an extinguished flame. This site's other pages sometimes render the same Pali word ("nirodha") as "cessation" instead -- same concept, different sentence.
*[Tathāgata]: A title for the Buddha, traditionally left untranslated. It means roughly "the one who has arrived at things as they truly are."
*[unwholesome]: This project's rendering of "akusala" -- roughly, mentally and ethically harmful: blameworthy, leads to harm, and is criticized by people with good judgment.
*[wholesome]: This project's rendering of "kusala" -- roughly, mentally and ethically healthy: blameless, leads to well-being, and is praised by people with good judgment.
*[world]: A common word in these texts that shifts meaning by context -- sometimes the physical cosmos beings are reborn into, sometimes (as in MN 63) a specific philosophical question about whether existence as a whole is eternal or finite. Each sutta's own framing makes clear which sense is meant.
